title: Microbiology: bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites
note: Bacteria are prokaryotes with 70S ribosomes and, in most, a peptidoglycan wall; the Gram stain sorts them by that wall. Viruses are acellular and replicate only inside host cells. Fungi and parasites are eukaryotes, so they share more machinery with human cells, which makes them harder to target.

read.title: What the Gram stain reveals
text: The Gram stain, developed in the 1880s, is still one of the first tests run on a bacterial sample, because it sorts most bacteria into two groups in minutes. A heat-fixed smear is flooded with crystal violet, which turns every cell purple. Gram's iodine is added next as a mordant; it forms a large complex with the dye.

The key step is decolorizing with alcohol or an acetone-alcohol mix. Gram-positive bacteria have a thick wall of peptidoglycan that traps the dye complex, so they stay purple. Gram-negative bacteria have only a thin peptidoglycan layer beneath an outer membrane, and the alcohol washes the dye out. A final counterstain, safranin, colors these decolorized cells pink or red.

The result matters clinically. The gram-negative outer membrane contains lipopolysaccharide, an endotoxin that can trigger fever and inflammation, and it acts as a barrier that keeps some drugs out. The thick gram-positive wall, by contrast, is exposed and is a direct target for drugs that block wall synthesis. A quick stain therefore narrows the list of likely organisms and helps guide early treatment while slower tests are pending.
